title: Mural on the Stepped Wall
story: A school courtyard has an old garden wall built from columns of bricks, each column one brick wide, standing side by side with no gaps between them. Over the years some columns lost bricks, so the top of the wall is a jagged staircase. A column with height 0 has lost all its bricks.

The art class wants to paint the biggest possible rectangular mural on the wall. The rectangle must sit on the ground, cover whole columns side by side, and stay on bricks: it cannot rise above the shortest column it spans.
task: Write largestMural(heights). heights[i] is the number of bricks in column i, and each brick is 1 × 1. Return the largest area, in bricks, of a rectangle that spans one or more consecutive columns and is no taller than the shortest of them.
Return 0 for an empty wall or a wall with no bricks at all.

examples.explanation: Columns 0 to 2 (heights 3, 5, 4) are all at least 3 tall, giving 3 × 3 = 9. The tallest column alone gives only 6, and columns 1 and 2 give 4 × 2 = 8. Any rectangle that includes column 3 is at most 1 brick tall: 1 × 6 = 6.
Columns 1 and 2 give 4 × 2 = 8. Column 3 has no bricks, so no rectangle can cross it, and the 5 on its own is only 5.

hints: Fix one column, say the 4 in [3, 5, 4, 1, 6, 2], and say the mural must be exactly as tall as that column. How far left and right can the mural stretch?

Every best mural is exactly as tall as its shortest column. So for each column, you want the widest rectangle of that column's height: it stretches until it hits a shorter column on each side. The answer is the best of these n candidates.
So for each column you need the nearest shorter column on the left and on the right. That is a "next smaller" question, which a stack of columns with increasing heights answers in one pass.

Walk left to right with a stack of indexes whose heights increase. When column i is shorter than the top, pop the top: i is its right limit, and the new top of the stack (or -1 if empty) is its left limit, so its area is height × (i - left - 1). Push i. At the end, treat one extra column of height 0 to pop everything left.
bruteForce: Try every pair of start and end columns, keep a running minimum height as the end moves right, and compute minimum × width.

That is O(n²): about 5 billion pairs for a wall of 100,000 columns. Most of the work is wasted because a run of columns is rechecked from every starting point. The insight is that each column only needs to know where it is blocked on each side.

tests.note: flat wall: use the full width
rising: 3 x 3 = 9 beats the tallest column
the low middle column spans everything
tall thin column beats the long low strip
long low strip beats the tall column
equal heights next to each other

js: const stack = []; // indexes; heights increase from bottom to top
const h = i < heights.length ? heights[i] : 0; // a final 0 flushes the stack
// shorter neighbours: left is the new top, right is i
py: stack = []  # indexes; heights increase from bottom to top
h = heights[i] if i < len(heights) else 0  # a final 0 flushes the stack
# shorter neighbours: left is the new top, right is i
walkthrough: The best mural is as tall as its shortest column. So try each column as "the shortest": its mural spreads sideways until it meets a shorter column on each side. A stack of increasing heights finds both limits. When a shorter column arrives and pops a column off the stack, that newcomer is the popped column's right limit, and the column now below it on the stack is its left limit.
• i = 0, 1: heights 3 and 5 keep increasing. Push both. Stack: 0(3), 1(5).
• i = 2 (4). 5 ≥ 4: pop 1. Left limit 0, right limit 2, width 1. Area 5 × 1 = 5. Push. Stack: 0(3), 2(4).
• i = 3 (1). Pop 2: left 0, width 3 - 0 - 1 = 2, area 4 × 2 = 8. Pop 0: stack empty so left = -1, width 3, area 3 × 3 = 9. Push. Stack: 3(1).
• i = 5 (2). Pop 4: left 3, width 1, area 6. Push. Stack: 3(1), 5(2).
• i = 6, the extra 0. Pop 5: left 3, width 2, area 4. Pop 3: left -1, width 6, area 6.

The best area seen is 9. Two details matter. The final height-0 step flushes columns that never met a shorter one. And when a column is popped, the area uses the index below it on the stack, not its own index, because every column between them was taller and already popped.
solution.timeWhy: Each index is pushed once and popped once.
solution.spaceWhy: A rising wall keeps every index on the stack until the end.
solution.takeaway: When the answer for an element depends on how far it can stretch before hitting something smaller (or bigger), use a monotonic stack: the moment an element is popped, you know both of its limits. This also solves the largest rectangle of 1s in a grid, one row at a time.
